PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 7

The critical density, and the density parameter Ω

Rather than working with the physical density, cosmologists usually specify the density of the Universe as a dimensionless parameter, which is defined as the ratio of ρ to the critical density. The critical density ρc is the special value which fixes the geometry of the Universe to be flat. We can derive the critical density from the Friedmann equation as follows. We write the Friedmann equation as

H2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ-k⁢c2a2 (1)

From this form it is immediately obvious that for a given value of H, there is a critical density ρc which makes the Universe flat. If we set k=0 we see that

ρc⁢(t)=3⁢H28⁢π⁢G (2)

The Hubble parameter and the critical density are both functions of time, and if we adopt the usual notation that H0=100⁢hkm s-1 Mpc-1, then the present-day critical density is

ρc⁢(t0)=1.88⁢h2×10-26⁢kg⁢m-3 (3)

The Universe need not be flat (though it turns out that it probably is!), but the critical density provides us with a reference scale for measuring cosmological densities. Rather than giving a physical density, we usually work with the dimensionless parameter Ω:

Ω⁢(t)=ρ⁢(t)ρc (4)

Different density parameters are used to denote the various different contributions to the density, and the choice of notation here is not always consistent. In this course we will use Ωm to refer to the matter density and Ω to refer to the total density (i.e., the sum of all the different contributions), with additional subscripts 0 to denote present-day values111 This is consistent with the modern literature, but slightly different from Liddle’s textbook.. We can substitute for the critical density in Equation 1 to find

H2=H2⁢Ω-k⁢c2a2 (5)

and therefore

Ω-1=k⁢c2H2⁢a2 (6)

This makes it explicit that Ω=1 (which is another way of writing ρ=ρc) is the special value which sets k=0: this is known as a critical-density Universe. And as k is a constant, a critical density Universe remains critical (with Ω=1) with time, even though the physical value of ρc decreases as the Universe expands222 Some authors use Equation 6 to define a “density parameter” associated with the curvature: Ω+Ωk=1, where Ωk=-k⁢c2/H2⁢a2 is a dimensionless measure of the curvature. The latest (2018) results from the Planck satellite find Ωk=0.001±0.002. The data are therefore consistent with a flat Universe, and the maximum allowed curvature (within the observational/experimental uncertainties) is very small..

The deceleration parameter

We began this course with the observation that Universe is expanding, but we now also understand that the expansion rate (i.e., the Hubble parameter) is changing with time. The standard way of quantifying this is in terms of the deceleration parameter q0, which is defined as follows. We begin with a Taylor series expansion of the scale factor a⁢(t) about the present time t0:

a⁢(t)=a⁢(t0)+a˙⁢(t0)⁢(t-t0)+12⁢a¨⁢(t0)⁢(t-t0)2+O⁢(t3) (7)

If we then divide through by a⁢(t0), and neglect terms of order t3 and above, we find

a⁢(t)a⁢(t0)=1+H0⁢(t-t0)+12⁢a¨⁢(t0)a⁢(t0) (8)

We then write this equation as

a⁢(t)a⁢(t0)=1+H0⁢(t-t0)-q02⁢H02⁢(t-t0)2 (9)

where we have defined

q0=-a¨⁢(t0)a⁢(t0)⁢1H02=-a⁢(t0)⁢a¨⁢(t0)a˙2⁢(t0) (10)

q0 therefore measures the lowest-order deviation from a purely linear expansion. If we look back at the acceleration equation, we see immediately that q0 can be calculated directly from H0 and ρ and/or p (or equivalently from H0 and Ω0), so if we know the content of the Universe exactly then we can always compute q0. However, if the composition of the Universe is not known – which is usually the case – then q0 provides an alternative way of relating it to observable quantities.

Note also the negative sign in the definition: q0 is defined as a deceleration, because historically that was what was expected in a matter- or radiation-dominated Universe. However, observations in the late 1990s and early 2000s showed conclusively that q0 is negative333 The current best measurement of the deceleration parameter is q0≃-0.53., and that the Universe is actually accelerating. To explain this requires us to consider a new class of cosmological models.
